2.text: boat exclusively, a boat’s crew consisted of eight men, — one at the helm,

3.text: another at the prow with harpoon and lance, and six paddlers. The man at

4.text: the helm, who is the master of the boat, was sometimes considered as an

5.text: extra member; and the whole crew, counting the regular number of eight,

6.text: thus included nine men. The number eight was so firmly established, that

7.text: even the sea-werwolves (killer-whales), of which I have spoken before, were

8.text: supposed to course around in the sea in crews of eight.

9.text: At present, in many places on the Pacific shore, the American whaling-

10.text: boat has replaced the skin boat for hunting-purposes. The crew necessary

11.text: for the whaling-boat is smaller than that for the skin boat, consisting of only

12.text: five or six men, because the number of oarsmen required is less. The boat’s

13.text: crew is formed of the nearest relatives of the owner. It is a kind of family

14.text: co-operative group, the members hunting together and dividing the spoils.

15.text: The chief member, or head, of a boat’s crew, is called “boat-master”
15.note: Closing quote after boat-master printed as a straight mark in the draft; keyed curly per §1: “Quotation marks curly “…”, never straight.”

16.text: (äᵋttw-eˊrmečɪn), and is the owner of the boat. He constructs the skin boat
16.resolved: ä = a+U+0308; ᵋ = U+1D4B COMBINING LARYNGEAL (glottalization); eˊ = e + U+02CA (stress); č = c+U+030C; ɪ = U+026A
16.note: At 4x the vowel between rm and č shows a rounded, breve-shaped mark above it, visibly distinct in curvature from the caron over č immediately after it. §2.6 licenses U+0306 COMBINING BREVE only on u and i, never on e, so per R5 the plain catalogued letter e is keyed and the would-be mark is flagged uncatalogued for adjudication. Cf. the ratified form aᵋtw-eˊrmečɪn (“boat-master”) at 2-022, which carries no such mark, though that page's word also differs in its onset (atw vs. ttw, a vs. ä) so it is cited only as context, not as the reading.

17.text: through the efforts of his own small family, that living in his house. For

18.text: this he has to prepare, in the first place, a big walrus-hide and a sufficient

19.text: quantity of fresh, strong thong. Then he collects the wood necessary for the

20.text: frame, — a rather difficult task on those treeless shores. — or, if he is unable

21.text: to find driftwood of the required quality, he may buy a ready-made frame,

22.text: one of those which are made and sold on the American shore. The wooden
22.note: Draft appended a comma after 'wooden' not present on the page; line ends bare per R9, checked at 2x.

23.text: boat-frame and also parts of it are highly valued among the Chukchee. They

24.text: form objects of sale, are left as an inheritance, etc. If some part has deterior-

25.text: ated, it is replaced by a new one, and thus the frame may be kept in use

26.text: for two generations or more. Walrus skins and thongs, on the contrary, are

27.text: often changed, since every autumn, after the end of the sea-hunting season,

28.text: the skin cover is taken off from the frame and kept separately.

29.text: When the master of a boat is not rich enough to get all the material

30.text: necessary for a skin boat, two or three of his nearest relatives, usually brothers

31.text: or cousins, help him. Then they are all considered “boat’s masters.” The
31.note: Closing quote after masters printed as a straight mark in the draft; keyed curly per §1.

32.text: oldest of them sits at the helm and directs the hunting-expedition; but, if his

33.text: luck in hunting does not seem very great, he may give up his place to one

35.text: Whaling-boats are bought from the Americans or from local traders

36.text: who deal with American whalers. Whalebone, fawn-skins (black or spotted),

37.text: ready-made clothes of reindeer-skin, walrus-tusks, etc., are given in exchange

38.text: for it. Since the value of a whaling-boat is considerably greater than that

39.text: of a skin boat, being about twenty or thirty large slabs of whalebone, the

40.text: purchase of such a boat is difficult for one man. Still the question is practically
40.note: Draft appended a comma after 'practically' not present on the page; line ends bare per R9, checked at 2x.

41.text: decided by the success in whale-hunting. If at least one good whale has

42.text: been killed in a village, several families will be able to buy new whaling-boats

43.text: the next summer. If not, no whaling-boats are bought.

44.note: Draft keyed a plain hyphen; §2.11 sets the signature-line number unspaced against an em dash, U+2014.
